content: In HIV-infected individuals, oral candidiasis is a common condition, with prevalence rates reaching up to 81% in children. If left untreated, these lesions significantly contribute to the morbidity associated with HIV infection. Effective management of HIV-related oral candidiasis is essential to maintaining the quality of life for affected individuals. Clinically, oral candidiasis presents as a soft white coating or pseudomembrane on the mucosal surfaces of the mouth, which, when wiped off, reveals a red, raw surface. Other manifestations include depapillation or a red/raw appearance of the tongue, or thick white plaques that cannot be rubbed off, which are more challenging to diagnose. While Candida albicans is the most common causative organism, other species may also be involved. In cases of oropharyngeal candidiasis, dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) may indicate esophageal involvement, necessitating endoscopy for definitive diagnosis. Most patients with esophageal candidiasis respond to antifungal therapy within 3 to 7 days. However, if symptoms persist despite appropriate systemic antifungal treatment, endoscopy is recommended to rule out other causes, such as herpes simplex virus or cytomegalovirus esophagitis, which are common in immunocompromised populations. For treatment, oral fluconazole (100–150 mg daily for 7–14 days) is the preferred option for adults. If fluconazole is unavailable or contraindicated, alternatives include topical therapies such as nystatin suspension or pastilles, or clotrimazole troches. In children, oral fluconazole (3 mg/kg daily for 7–14 days) is also recommended as the first-line treatment. For mild cases in children, topical therapies like nystatin or clotrimazole are effective alternatives. Prompt initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) is strongly recommended for all HIV-infected individuals with oropharyngeal candidiasis, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, adolescents, and children. If there is no response to fluconazole after 14 days, higher doses may be considered, or resistance to fluconazole should be suspected. In such cases, itraconazole may be used as an alternative, but potential drug interactions must be carefully managed. For patients with swallowing difficulties, esophageal candidiasis should be considered, and treatment duration may need to be extended to 14–30 days. Maintenance therapy is not recommended, and the use of gentian violet is no longer advised due to lack of efficacy. In HIV-infected patients with oropharyngeal candidiasis, it is important to assess for dysphagia to rule out esophageal involvement, which requires systemic antifungal treatment. A diagnostic trial of systemic antifungal therapy is appropriate before performing endoscopy. Additionally, breastfeeding women with oropharyngeal candidiasis should have their breasts examined and treated if necessary. The systematic review of antifungal treatments for oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV-infected individuals found that fluconazole is highly effective, with clinical cure rates ranging from 87% to 100%. It is more effective than nystatin and clotrimazole in achieving clinical and mycological cures. However, the development of fluconazole-resistant Candida species and the cost of prophylaxis limit its feasibility for routine prevention. Therefore, antifungal prophylaxis is not recommended. Evidence for treatment in children is limited, but expert consensus supports the use of oral fluconazole as the preferred treatment. Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are rare but life-threatening skin disorders characterized by widespread epidermal necrosis. Mortality rates range from 1–5% for SJS and 25–30% for TEN. In HIV-infected patients, these conditions can occur both on and off ART, with sulfonamides, antituberculosis drugs (especially thiacetazone), and other medications being common triggers. SJS involves less than 10% body surface area (BSA) detachment, while TEN involves more than 30% BSA detachment. Overlap cases involve 10–30% BSA detachment. Management of SJS and TEN requires immediate discontinuation of the offending drug and supportive care. The use of systemic corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) remains controversial, with limited evidence supporting their effectiveness. In HIV-infected patients, corticosteroids may increase the risk of opportunistic infections and sepsis. Supportive care includes intravenous fluids, wound care, sepsis monitoring, and management of complications such as eye and skin issues. Early detection of SJS and TEN is critical, and healthcare providers should be vigilant for symptoms such as blistering, tenderness, redness, rash, and erosions. The evidence for specific treatments for SJS and TEN in HIV-infected individuals is of very low quality, with most studies being observational and involving small sample sizes. No randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted in this population. The high mortality rates associated with these conditions underscore the importance of early detection and supportive care. Implementation of these guidelines requires integration into existing HIV care programs and training for healthcare workers to recognize and manage these conditions. Laboratory services should be equipped to perform necessary diagnostic tests, such as skin scrapings and biopsies. Monitoring and evaluation of guideline implementation should be incorporated into national ART programs, with data collection on opportunistic conditions and treatment outcomes. Further research is needed to address gaps in knowledge, including the role of adjunctive therapies, prevention strategies, and the development of resistance to current treatments.
